abstract: Using data from over 3 million people, researchers trace the ancestral history of the EGFR T790M germline mutation and its present contribution to lung cancer risk in those who never smoked.

title: Prime editing goes large
abstract: A technique known as prime assembly expands the capabilities of prime editing, allowing larger genome rearrangements and potentially wider clinical applications.

title: Oral small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist safiglipron in early type 2 diabetes: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
authors: on behalf of the OUTSTAND-1 Investigator Group
abstract: Safiglipron is an oral small-molecule glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist administered without fasting or dietary restrictions. We evaluated its efficacy and safety in OUTSTAND-1, a phase 3, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial at 46 sites in China. We randomized 284 adults with type 2 diabetes managed with diet and exercise alone (mean baseline HbA1c 7.95%, median diabetes duration 1.6 years, 33.1% women) to once-daily safiglipron 30 mg ( n = 70), 60 mg ( n = 70), 90 mg ( n = 72) or placebo ( n = 72) for 32 weeks, followed by a 20-week active-treatment extension. For the primary endpoint, placebo-adjusted treatment differences in HbA1c change from baseline to week 32 were −1.22% (95% CI, −1.53 to −0.91), −1.20% (95% CI, −1.52 to −0.89) and −1.45% (95% CI, −1.75 to −1.14) for 30 mg, 60 mg and 90 mg, respectively (all P < 0.0001; treatment policy estimand). Secondary outcomes showed HbA1c < 7.0% in 71.4−77.8% versus 25.0%, HbA1c ≤ 6.5% in 58.6−68.1% versus 16.7% and placebo-adjusted fasting plasma glucose differences of −1.58, −1.68 and −2.08 mmol l − 1 , respectively (all P < 0.0001). Body weight differences were modest (−0.65%, −2.23% and −3.56% versus placebo). Other secondary outcomes generally favored safiglipron for HbA1c < 5.7% attainment, postprandial glycemia, homeostatic model assessment of β cell function (HOMA-β), homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR), disposition index and waist circumference, with less rescue therapy use. Insulin and C-peptide responses varied by dose, and changes in treatment satisfaction were limited. Gastrointestinal adverse events were most common and mostly mild or moderate. Adverse events led to treatment discontinuation in 1.4%, 2.9%, 6.9% and 0% of participants receiving safiglipron 30 mg, 60 mg, 90 mg and placebo, respectively. These findings support once-daily oral safiglipron as an effective treatment option for type 2 diabetes. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06672172 .

title: A synthetic lethal drug for microsatellite instability cancers
abstract: In a phase 1 trial, inhibition of the Werner syndrome helicase (WRN) enzyme exploits a new synthetic lethal vulnerability in cancers with microsatellite instability, offering a new way to target these tumors beyond immune checkpoint inhibition.

title: Reproducibility in biomedical research
abstract: Reproducibility has long been considered a foundation of trustworthy science, yet practices that enable reproducible research remain inconsistently implemented, despite widespread awareness and establishment of policies and guidelines. Biomedical research that cannot be reproduced can lead to resource waste and adversely impact patient safety, public health outcomes, scientific progress and public trust. Rapid advances in technology, scientific dissemination and clinical translation have prompted renewed emphasis on validating research methods and findings to ensure transparency, rigor and credibility. Here we provide an overview of the current landscape of reproducible research in the biomedical sciences, summarize current efforts to harmonize terminology and implementation, and highlight the persistent barriers to adoption of best practices. We outline a practical framework to promote more uniform implementation and explore future directions for advancing reproducibility across stakeholders in the research process, including researchers, institutions, journals and funders.

title: Werner helicase inhibitor for advanced microsatellite instability solid tumors: a phase 1 trial
abstract: Werner syndrome helicase (WRN) is a synthetic lethal target for microsatellite instability (MSI) cancers. In part 1 of this ongoing first-in-human, phase 1 trial, escalating doses of RO7589831 (VVD-133214), a first-in-class, WRN covalent inhibitor, were evaluated in 88 patients with MSI and/or deficient DNA mismatch repair advanced solid tumors. RO7589831 was administered once daily (150 mg), twice daily (BID; 150–1,000 mg) or three-times daily (TID; 200–600 mg). Primary objectives were to evaluate safety and tolerability, and identify the recommended phase 2 dose and schedule (RP2D). Secondary objectives included evaluation of antitumor activity (end points: disease control rate (DCR), objective response rate (ORR), duration of response (DOR), progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS)). One dose-limiting toxicity of grade 2 nausea occurred in the 600-mg TID cohort; however, the maximum tolerated dose was not identified per protocol. Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) occurring in ≥10% were mostly grade 1–2; events in ≥30% were nausea (54.5%, 48/88; grade 3+: 2.3%, 2/88), diarrhea (43.2%, 38/88; grade 3+: 1.1%, 1/88), fatigue (39.8%, 35/88; grade 3+: 2.3%, 2/88), anemia (37.5%, 33/88; grade 3+: 11.4%, 10/88), and vomiting (30.7%, 27/88, grade 3+: 1.1%, 1/88). TEAEs leading to RO7589831 discontinuation were uncommon (3.4%, 3/88). No grade 5 TEAEs occurred. The DCR among MSI efficacy-evaluable patients was 74.2% (49/66). Seven patients achieved confirmed RECIST v.1.1 partial responses (ORR 10.6%, 7/66); median DOR was 10.2+ months. Among MSI efficacy-evaluable patients, median PFS was 6.7 months (95% CI 4.1–8.5); median OS was 17.6 months (95% CI 17.6–not estimable). Although direct target engagement in tumor tissue could not be demonstrated, exploratory analyses of ctDNA molecular response and FDG-PET metabolic response supported biological activity. The 150-mg and 600-mg BID doses were selected as RP2Ds for dose optimization. These data suggest that RO7589831 has a manageable safety profile and warrants further clinical testing. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06004245 .

title: Intravenous hyaluronidase-expressing oncolytic adenovirus with chemotherapy in metastatic pancreatic cancer: a randomized phase 2b trial
abstract: Zabilugene almadenorepvec (VCN-01) is a hyaluronidase-expressing oncolytic adenovirus with a favorable safety profile and encouraging antitumor activity in patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. This randomized phase 2b trial evaluated the efficacy and safety of two doses of intravenous VCN-01 with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel (GnP) versus GnP alone as first-line therapy in metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. The primary endpoints were overall survival (OS) in the intent-to-treat and full analysis set (FAS) populations, and safety and tolerability in the safety population. In the intent-to-treat population (VCN-01 + GnP, n = 53; GnP, n = 48), median OS in the VCN-01 + GnP versus GnP group was 10.6 versus 8.6 months (hazard ratio (HR) = 0.69 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.42–1.12), P = 0.196) and progression-free survival was 5.6 versus 4.6 months (HR = 0.63 (95% CI 0.4–1.00), P = 0.046). In the FAS population ( n = 48 per group), median OS was 10.8 months in the VCN-01 + GnP group versus 8.6 months in the GnP group (HR = 0.57 (95% CI 0.34-0.96), P = 0.055) and progression-free survival was 7.0 versus 4.6 months (HR = 0.55 (95% CI, 0.34-0.88), P = 0.011). The primary efficacy endpoint of OS was met in the FAS population. Duration of response was 11.2 versus 5.4 months (HR = 0.22 (95% CI 0.08–0.63), P = 0.004). No statistically significant differences were observed in overall response rate, disease control rate or carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels between treatment groups. In addition, survival rates in the VCN-01 + GnP group versus the GnP group were 35.5% versus 12.8% at 15 months, and 31.1% versus 8.5% at 18 months. Patients receiving two VCN-01 doses 14 weeks apart showed greater survival benefit, with sustained circulating viral genomes indicating ongoing viral replication and preserved second-dose bioactivity despite persistent neutralizing antibodies. More frequent VCN-01-related events included pyrexia, flu-like symptoms, elevation in liver enzymes and decreases in platelet counts, with serious events occurring in 22.6% of patients. Milder toxicity was observed after the second administration. Two fatal events occurred, one in each treatment group; neither was considered related to study treatment. These results further support VCN-01 combined with GnP as a first-line therapy for metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and warrant evaluation in a blinded phase 3 trial. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05673811 .

title: Effects of semaglutide on kidney disease in type 2 diabetes: a randomized placebo-controlled trial
abstract: The GLP-1 receptor agonist semaglutide preserves kidney function in people with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease, but the underlying mechanisms are unclear. Here we report a 52-week randomized trial of subcutaneous semaglutide 1 mg once weekly versus placebo ( n = 106 ( n = 25 women, n = 81 men)) in participants with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease. To identify kidney-specific mechanisms of action for semaglutide, we performed integrated multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging of the kidney and biopsy for histology ( n = 33), alongside single-nucleus ( n = 22) and spatial transcriptomics ( n = 13) on paired samples with before- and after-treatment measurements. Coprimary magnetic resonance imaging outcomes (oxygenation by R2*, global perfusion and tissue inflammation by T1 mapping) were not significantly altered by semaglutide versus placebo treatment. Secondary outcomes revealed that semaglutide treatment, as compared to placebo, was associated with a significantly reduced renal artery resistive index and stabilization of the apparent diffusion coefficient, indicating prevention of fibrosis progression. Moreover, secondary transcriptomic outcomes revealed pronounced effects of semaglutide on glomerular endothelial cells, consistent with the results of spatial analyses indicating reduced numbers of immune cells in the proximity of these endothelial cells. The results from this trial indicate that mechanisms of kidney protection by semaglutide may include reduced vascular resistance, prevention of fibrosis and improved underlying molecular programs promoting endothelial cell health. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04865770 .

title: Five-year survival with neoadjuvant therapy in melanoma: updated pooled analysis from the International Neoadjuvant Melanoma Consortium (INMC)
authors: Astrid A. M. van der Veldt
abstract: Neoadjuvant immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are standard of care for resectable stage IIIB–D melanoma, but knowledge gaps remain regarding optimal treatment type, long-term survival, postsurgical management and clinical, histopathological or molecular subgroups. We analyzed 1,038 patients treated with neoadjuvant ICIs ( n = 735), BRAF and MEK inhibitors (BRAF/MEKis; n = 119) or ICI plus any targeted therapy (ICI + TT; n = 184) from 26 international sites in both trial (755, 72.7%) and nontrial (283, 27.3%) settings. ICI regimens included anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) alone (PD-1 alone; n = 242) and anti-PD-1 plus other immuno-oncology agent(s) (PD-1 + IO; n = 489). Outcomes included major pathological response (MPR), recurrence-free survival (RFS) and overall survival (OS). An MPR was achieved in 57.8% of patients with ICIs, 51.4% with BRAF/MEKis and 44.6% with ICI + TT. PD-1 + IO elicited higher MPR rates than PD-1 alone (61.4% versus 49.5%). The 5-year RFS rate was 61.0% with PD-1 alone, 73.9% with PD-1 + IO, 37.4% with BRAF/MEKis and 76.4% with ICI + TT; the 5-year OS rates were 83.3%, 87.5%, 69.8% and 83.9%, respectively. ICI-treated patients with MPR had 5-year OS rates of 98.8% with PD-1 alone and 97.9% with PD-1 + IO and gained no benefit from continuing ICIs into the adjuvant setting. Neoadjuvant ICIs were active in BRAF -mutant melanoma (MPR, 46.3%), acral melanoma (38.1%), in-transit metastases (66.7%) and oligometastases (41.2%), although subgroup sizes and relative effectiveness varied. Survival outcomes were excellent with neoadjuvant ICIs, particularly in patients achieving MPR, but poor with BRAF/MEKis and mixed with ICI + TT. Predictive biomarker-driven trials, effective adjuvant strategies and subgroup-specific research are needed for nonresponders.

title: Urine cell-free RNA for bladder cancer detection and treatment response prediction
abstract: Urine biomarkers promise to improve noninvasive detection and molecular characterization of genitourinary malignancies. Here we describe urine random priming and affinity capture of cell-free RNA (cfRNA) fragments for enrichment analysis by sequencing (uRARE-seq), a liquid biopsy method for urine cfRNA profiling, and apply it to 683 urine samples from patients with cancer and controls. Urine cfRNA contained transcripts from genitourinary tissues and, in patients with prostate, kidney or bladder cancer, tumor-derived transcripts. uRARE-seq demonstrated 95% sensitivity at 90% specificity for detecting localized bladder cancer. The method outperformed urine tumor DNA analysis and was unaffected by the presence of field-effect mutations. Urine cfRNA analysis also sensitively detected minimal residual disease and distinguished complete molecular responses after surgery from those after intravesical Bacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG). Pretreatment urine from complete responders to BCG was enriched for T cell and other immune signatures, suggesting a preexisting antitumor immune response, whereas nonresponders showed higher expression of proliferation-related genes. In pretreatment urine from 114 patients, this biological difference enabled development of a biomarker predicting likelihood of response to BCG versus chemotherapy (area under the curve 0.93) that was strongly associated with risk of recurrence. Urine cfRNA analysis is therefore a promising biomarker approach for bladder cancer and potentially other urologic malignancies, although prospective studies are needed to assess its clinical utility.

title: Small quantity lipid-based nutritional supplementation and measles vaccination coverage in children aged 6−23 months: a pragmatic cluster-randomized trial
abstract: Undernutrition and infectious diseases pose a double threat to child survival, especially in areas with a high malnutrition burden and low vaccination coverage. In this study, we evaluated whether distributing preventive small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) alongside routine immunization services may increase vaccine uptake in a pediatric, pragmatic, cluster-randomized controlled trial in northern Nigeria. Twenty geographically defined clusters across two Local Government Areas were randomized 1:1 to the NutriVax strategy (intervention) or standard National Program of Immunization (NPI) services (control). NutriVax provided a monthly ration of SQ-LNS to children aged 6−23 months after routine NPI delivery at primary healthcare centers. The primary outcome was coverage of the first dose of measles-containing vaccine (MCV1) verified by vaccination card among children aged 12−23 months, assessed in an endline population-based household cross-sectional survey 12 months after conducting a similar baseline survey. The endline survey included 1,604 children (801 control, 803 NutriVax); 48% of children surveyed in intervention clusters had ever received SQ-LNS. The odds of receiving card-verified MCV1 were two times higher in the NutriVax arm than in the control arm (odds ratio = 2.08, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.30−3.35, P = 0.004). The difference-in-differences, cluster conditional analysis indicated a 20.1 percentage-point (pp) increase in MCV1 coverage from baseline (95% CI: 13.7−26.5 pp, P < 0.0001) relative to the control arm. Co-delivering SQ-LNS with routine immunization substantially improved card-verified MCV1 uptake, supporting a scalable strategy to make progress toward targets set by the World Health Organizationʼs Immunization Agenda 2030 in similar settings. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06387511 .

title: The missing links in agentic AI autonomy
abstract: A new study tackles issues around operational and decisional trust of agentic artificial intelligence (AI), using locally deployed, on-premise agents and consistency-based gating to refer uncertain cases — but what happens after referral remains untested.

title: Oral small-molecule GLP-1RA safiglipron versus dapagliflozin in type 2 diabetes: a randomized, double-blind, active-comparator-controlled phase 3 trial
authors: on behalf of the OUTSTAND-2 Investigator Group
abstract: Safiglipron is an oral small-molecule glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist administered without fasting or dietary restrictions. We evaluated its efficacy and safety versus dapagliflozin in OUTSTAND-2, a phase 3, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, active-comparator-controlled trial conducted at 98 sites in China. We randomized 810 adults (mean hemoglobin A1C (HbA1c) 8.60%, median diabetes duration 5.0 years, 35.7% women) to safiglipron 30 mg ( n = 202), safiglipron 60 mg ( n = 203), safiglipron 90 mg ( n = 203) or dapagliflozin 10 mg ( n = 202) for 32 weeks, followed by a 20-week active-treatment extension. For the primary endpoint, treatment differences versus dapagliflozin in change from baseline in HbA1c at week 32 under the primary non-inferiority estimand were −0.30% (95% confidence interval (CI): −0.51 to −0.09), −0.22% (−0.44 to −0.01) and −0.40% (−0.62 to −0.19) for safiglipron 30 mg, 60 mg and 90 mg, respectively, establishing non-inferiority for all three doses (all P < 0.0001; non-inferiority margin 0.4%). Under the treatment policy estimand, 90 mg met the prespecified statistical criterion for superiority (difference −0.25%; 95% CI: −0.45 to −0.05; one-sided P = 0.0067), whereas 60 mg did not ( P = 0.0789), after which fixed-sequence testing stopped. HbA1c target attainment rates with safiglipron versus dapagliflozin were 54.9−63.5% versus 36.5% for HbA1c <7.0% and 38.9−48.6% versus 16.1% for HbA1c ≤6.5%. Mean body weight changes were −2.35%, −3.55%, −4.17% and −3.60% for safiglipron 30 mg, safiglipron 60 mg, safiglipron 90 mg and dapagliflozin, respectively. Fasting plasma glucose, seven-point self-monitored blood glucose profiles, waist circumference, HOMA-β, HOMA-IR and changes in treatment satisfaction showed varying degrees of improvement from baseline with both safiglipron and dapagliflozin. Rescue therapy was used by 0.5−1.5% versus 0% of participants, respectively. Gastrointestinal adverse events were more frequent with safiglipron and mostly mild or moderate; adverse events led to treatment discontinuation in 4.0%, 4.0%, 3.9% and 1.5% of participants, respectively. Safiglipron provides an effective oral treatment option for adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled with metformin. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06589765 .

title: Global and regional reference curves for pain across the lifespan in 6.1 million individuals in 118 countries
abstract: Pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide, yet no harmonized self-reported reference framework exists to characterize how its burden is distributed across the lifespan and world regions. In this study, we harmonized individual-level self-reported pain data from 6,125,459 participants across 902 population-based data sources in 118 countries to establish global reference trajectories of pain. We implemented these trajectories in an open-access benchmarking platform for positioning external datasets against global pain norms. Pain prevalence ranged from roughly 2% for facial pain to 40% for back pain, was consistently higher in women across all 11 anatomical sites (risk ratio range: 1.08−1.83) and increased most steeply before age 55 years. Contrary to existing estimates that generally project higher prevalence of pain conditions in higher Human Development Index (HDI) regions, we found that individuals in the lowest HDI countries experienced a substantially higher late-life prevalence of any bodily pain than those in the highest (risk difference: 30.6 percentage points (95% confidence interval: 26.9−34.3)), with low back pain approaching twice the prevalence at the oldest ages. Globally, 18.3% of pain burden across anatomical sites was attributable to three modifiable risk factors (smoking, obesity and low income), but this varied from 12.6% in sub-Saharan Africa to 27.1% in eastern Europe, indicating that the factors underlying pain in lower-HDI settings remain poorly characterized. Together, these reference trajectories provide a common framework for defining and comparing pain burden and informing more equitable global surveillance and prevention.

title: Extended follow-up of in vivo BCMA CAR-T therapy in relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma
abstract: Data on long-term outcomes of in vivo chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR‑T) therapy remain scarce. We previously reported preliminary safety and efficacy data of in vivo B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA) CAR‑T (ESO-T01), in four patients with relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma, without leukapheresis and lymphodepletion, with up to 3 months of follow-up. The primary endpoints included safety and tolerability, while the secondary endpoints comprised efficacy, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. All patients developed dual-phase cytokine release syndrome (grades 1–3) and hematotoxicities (grade ≥3). One patient developed grade 1 immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome. The objective response rate reached 100% (two stringent complete response and two partial response). Here we update the data on long‑term safety and response durability with a maximal follow‑up of 15 months. No immunogenicity‑ or integration‑related toxicities occurred, and no important adverse events related to ESO-T01 emerged beyond the initial report. Of the four patients, one maintained stringent complete response for 15 months. The median progression-free survival was 4.0 (range 3.0–15.0) months. After progression, diverse salvage therapies extended overall survival to 5.5–10.9 months after infusion. Three patients experienced relapse or progression, all with extramedullary involvement, and eventually died during follow-up. One patient achieved durable response with robust expansion from ex vivo CAR-T. Collectively, these updated results provide additional insights on the safety and efficacy of in vivo CAR-T therapies. The limited persistence observed necessitates the further optimization of the in vivo CAR-T platform. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06691685 .

title: An open vision-language model for diverse medical applications
abstract: Artificial intelligence has high potential for impact in healthcare applications, but its training and deployment are challenging due to diverse data, a complex spectrum of possible tasks and important privacy needs. High-performing foundation models that enable data-efficient fine-tuning for diverse downstream tasks can meaningfully accelerate development in this domain. We introduce MedGemma, a collection of medical vision-language foundation models based on Gemma 3. MedGemma demonstrates advanced medical understanding and reasoning across images and text and multiple medical imaging domains, exceeding the performance of similarly sized generative models while maintaining the general capabilities of the Gemma base models. For out-of-distribution tasks, MedGemma achieves improvements of 2.6–10% in medical image question answering, 15.5–18.1% in chest X-ray finding classification and 10.8% in agentic evaluations compared with the base models. Our results show that fine-tuning MedGemma can be more effective than fine-tuning the base Gemma 3 model for medical tasks, particularly in the setting of limited training data. We additionally introduce MedSigLIP, a medically tuned vision encoder derived from SigLIP. MedSigLIP powers the visual understanding capabilities of MedGemma and, as an encoder, achieves performance comparable to or better than that of many specialized medical image encoders. Taken together, the MedGemma collection provides a strong foundation of medical image and text capabilities, with the potential to accelerate medical research and the development of downstream applications.

title: MAGIC: an international network for evaluating generative artificial intelligence in global health
Author Correction: Natural killer T cells and CD8+ T cells are dispensable for T cell–dependent allergic airway inflammation
AI-assisted scoping review of code sharing in clinical prediction model research
abstract: Clinical prediction models are increasingly deployed to support diagnostic and prognostic decisions, making reproducibility essential for assessing their reliability and generalizability. Analytical code supports independent assessment of these processes, yet its availability in the literature remains limited. This scoping review quantifies current practices in sharing analytical code to inform the development of TRIPOD-Code, a reporting guideline for code availability and reproducibility. Here a large-language-model-assisted pipeline was developed to screen articles citing TRIPOD or TRIPOD+AI, extract repository links and assess retrieved repositories against 14 predefined reproducibility-related features. Among 3,967 articles, 482 (12.2%) included code-sharing statements. Sharing prevalence varied widely by journal and country. Repository assessment showed substantial heterogeneity in reproducibility features. These findings underscore the need for clearer expectations beyond code availability, including documentation, dependency specification and executable structure. Strengthening these practices may improve the usability of clinical prediction model studies and support their deployment in real-world clinical settings.

title: Addendum: Aberrant epithelial GREM1 expression initiates colonic tumorigenesis from cells outside the stem cell niche
A health-system-scale, episode-resolved multimodal atlas of cancer cachexia
abstract: Cancer cachexia is a wasting syndrome with outsized impact on morbidity and mortality, yet its drivers and systemic consequences remain poorly defined. In this study, we repurposed longitudinal clinicogenomic data from 52,236 patients with cancer profiled by MSK-IMPACT (2010–2024) at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center to define episode-resolved trajectories of consensus-defined cachectic weight loss and linked these events to outcomes, serology and tumor genotypes. Cachectic episodes clustered near periods of disease progression and were associated with inferior outcomes in nearly all cancer types. Across diverse malignancies, cachectic weight loss episodes exhibited a consistent serologic signature characterized by lower albumin and hemoglobin and higher levels of liver enzymes. Numerous somatic tumor genotypes, including TP53 mutation across several diseases, were also associated with more frequent onset of cachectic episodes. Motivated by these observations, we developed a multivariate model to predict impending risk of cachectic weight loss in patients with lung, colorectal and prostate cancer, validated in an independent, external cohort from Dana-Farber Cancer Institute ( n = 5,785). Routine clinicogenomic data are, therefore, a scalable resource for discovery in cancer cachexia.

title: Population-scale reconstruction of menopause dynamics reveals a physiological cliff at the final menstrual period
abstract: Menopause reshapes female physiology, yet current understanding is limited by small longitudinal cohorts that characterize it as a gradual transition. Large-scale biomedical datasets remain underutilized because the final menstrual period (FMP) age is rarely recorded. Here we present a computational framework, inspired by astronomy, that reconstructs FMP-anchored trajectories from cross-sectional data by removing the blurring caused by variation in FMP age across individuals. Applying this to two independent cohorts totaling 300 million laboratory tests revealed a step-like physiological cliff at the FMP including endocrine, skeletal, hepatic, renal and lipid systems. These discontinuities are absent in male individuals, are concordant across populations and appear markedly attenuated by menopausal hormone therapy. Dysregulation began more than a decade before FMP. These findings support a systemic, quantifiable view of menopause and provide a generalizable strategy for recovering hidden biological trajectories applicable to other transitions such as puberty or disease progression.

title: Characterizing the onset and progression of cancer cachexia using routine clinical data
abstract: In 52,236 patients with cancer, cachectic weight loss episodes were linked to lower survival rates, occurred at times of disease progression, and carried a consistent serological signature across routine laboratory markers. Specific tumor genotypes, including TP53 mutations, were also positively associated with cachexia risk. Statistical models were trained to predict a patient’s impending risk of cachexia.

title: Autologous and broadly neutralizing antibodies drive ART-free HIV control
abstract: A secondary analysis of trial data shows that both host antibodies and infused antibodies against HIV help to delay viral rebound after interruption of antiretroviral therapy (ART), which could inform approaches to durable, ART-free HIV control.

title: Human–artificial intelligence collaboration for comanaging epilepsy in real time
abstract: One-third of the world’s 70 million people with epilepsy have seizures uncontrolled by medication, and implantable devices are a promising treatment. These devices can detect impending seizures, missed medication and impaired cognition, but, like most medical devices, they cannot share this information with patients in real time. This is a missed opportunity for devices to learn from clinical events and teach patients how their behaviors affect their health. Here we present a device platform that converses with patients to help them manage their epilepsy. The inpatient prototype links scalp and intracranial electroencephalography (EEG) to a secure, large language model-based artificial intelligence (AI) that communicates bidirectionally through a smartphone app. The AI processes biomarkers of sleep, medication, cognition and seizure probability, notifies patients of clinical events and trends, records symptoms and responses, and uses their feedback to retrain its seizure detector, reducing false alarms. We validated this platform in 13 patients who are undergoing video-EEG monitoring for epilepsy (scalp, n = 11; intracranial, n = 2). In a pseudoprospective simulation, seizure detectors improved precision from patient feedback alone, without expert intervention. We propose this system as a scalable, safeguarded platform for medical devices that can rapidly adapt to patient and provider needs across epilepsy and other medical conditions.

title: Personalized neoantigen-targeting cancer vaccines in ovarian cancer: a phase 1 trial
abstract: Personalized neoantigen-targeting cancer vaccines in the adjuvant setting are of increasing interest across malignancies. Here we report the results of a phase 1 clinical trial testing the feasibility and safety of personalized neoantigen-targeting cancer vaccines for high-grade epithelial ovarian cancer. ‘NeoVax’ consisted of pools of synthetic long peptides targeting patient-specific neoantigens admixed with the immunostimulant poly-ICLC, was combined with delayed administration of anti-PD-1 antibody, and was tested in ten patients (one newly diagnosed patient (Cohort A) and nine patients at first recurrence (Cohort B)) with platinum-sensitive ovarian cancer following standard-of-care platinum doublet chemotherapy. Nine of 12 evaluable Cohort B patients were vaccinated (75%, 90% CI 47–93%) and 1 of 9 Cohort A patients (11%, 90% CI 0.6–43%). No unexpected safety signals were encountered and no patients discontinued treatment due to toxicity. Across patients, >70% selected targets remained detectable by noninvasive cell-free DNA analysis despite a median of 6.5 months from the time of diagnostic biopsy to vaccine administration, during which, patients received standard-of-care chemotherapy. Biomarker analysis was suggestive of biologic activity of the vaccine in six of ten patients and this was associated with broader tumor and vaccine-specific immune responses in blood and tumor following vaccination. Resistant tumor clones reflected diverse mechanisms affecting antigen presentation, indicative of immune-selective pressure exerted by vaccination. Overall, the interplay between the repertoire of antigens presented by the tumor and the breadth of induced immunity seemed to dictate clinical efficacy following vaccination. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04024878 .

title: Talazoparib plus enzalutamide in high-volume metastatic hormone-naive prostate cancer: a randomized phase 2 trial
abstract: Combining inhibition of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase and androgen receptor (AR) pathway has demonstrated clinical activity in men with metastatic prostate cancer, although the extent of benefit in tumors lacking homologous recombination repair ( HRR ) gene alterations remains uncertain. We conducted a randomized phase 2 trial evaluating talazoparib plus enzalutamide versus enzalutamide alone in men with high-volume metastatic hormone-naive prostate cancer (mHNPC). Fifty-four patients starting androgen deprivation therapy received two cycles of enzalutamide lead-in before 1:2 randomization to enzalutamide ( n = 17) or enzalutamide plus talazoparib ( n = 37). The primary endpoint was met, with a 73% prostate-specific antigen (PSA) <0.2 ng ml −1 response rate at 12 months in the combination arm (95% confidence interval (CI) = 56–86%), exceeding the prespecified efficacy threshold ( P < 0.001); the PSA <0.2 rate in the control arm was 64.7% (95% CI = 38–86%, P = 0.54 for exploratory comparison between arms). Grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 68% patients receiving the combination versus 35% with enzalutamide alone, predominantly anemia (41%). Two fatal therapy-emergent myeloid neoplasms occurred in the enzalutamide plus talazoparib arm in patients with underlying genomic susceptibility. Analyses of paired tumor biopsies acquired at baseline and during enzalutamide lead-in phase demonstrated marked tumor transcriptional reprogramming after AR inhibition, including suppression of proliferation-associated and HRR-related gene expression programs, but without functional impairment of homologous recombination activity. Overall, talazoparib plus enzalutamide demonstrated clinical activity in patients with high-volume mHNPC but did not establish clear additional clinical benefit over enzalutamide alone in this biomarker-unselected population, while being associated with increased toxicity. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04332744 .

title: Making AI work in healthcare
abstract: Drawing on experiences across diverse settings, this issue of Nature Medicine explores the challenges of and lessons learned from the deployment of artificial intelligence models into healthcare.

title: Editorial Expression of Concern: Thyroid hormone inhibits lung fibrosis in mice by improving epithelial mitochondrial function
Hidden race disparities in cancer treatment toxicity
abstract: Large-scale analysis of real-world data reveals racial disparities in the occurrence of immune-related adverse events during cancer immunotherapy — which were not evident in trial data, owing to the enrollment of mostly white patients.

title: Optogenetic therapy shows early promise for treating retinitis pigmentosa
abstract: In a small study involving patients with blindness due to advanced retinitis pigmentosa, optogenetic therapy appears safe; early efficacy signals are promising and reveal opportunities for technical refinement.

title: Only time will tell
abstract: Chronotherapy promises to improve medicine by aligning treatment with the body’s internal clock. As this idea moves into clinical trials, a high-profile retraction reveals the ups and downs of circadian medicine.

title: EGFR-targeted antibody−toxin conjugate in recurrent glioma: a phase 1 trial
abstract: D2C7-ATC is a recombinant antibody−toxin conjugate (ATC) targeting wild-type epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and mutant EGFR variant III (EGFRvIII). We conducted a single-arm, single-site, open-label phase 1 trial evaluating a single infusion of D2C7-ATC via convection-enhanced delivery in the enhancing disease of 81 patients with biopsy-confirmed recurrent malignant glioma. The primary objective was to determine toxicity and the recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D) of D2C7-ATC. Secondary objectives included describing overall survival (OS) and assessing the association between EGFR expression and OS. The median overall survival (mOS) was 7.9 months among 72 patients with isocitrate dehydrogenase wild-type recurrent glioblastoma (IDHwt rGBM), including 35 patients in the dose-escalation stage (40 to 35,032 ng ml −1 ) and 37 patients in the dose-expansion stage (RP2D of 6,920 ng ml −1 ). D2C7-ATC was generally well tolerated, with mainly grade 1−2 treatment-related adverse events (67%). The maximum tolerated dose was exceeded at 35,032 ng ml −1 , where four patients experienced dose-limiting toxicities, including grade 4 ( N = 2) and grade 3 ( N = 2) events. Eight patients died on trial; all deaths were unrelated to D2C7-ATC. Univariate analyses identified survival-associated biomarkers, including tumor D2C7 antibody reactivity, circulating cytokines, a tumor inflammatory gene signature and neutrophils, monocytes and lymphocytes in blood. Notably, patients with IDHwt rGBM with a D2C7 antibody reactivity score of <1.5+ in pre-treatment tumor had an mOS of 17.38 months, whereas those with low IL-8 in post-treatment plasma had an mOS of 16.6 months. These findings indicate that EGFR-targeted D2C7-ATC therapy prolongs survival in a subset of patients with IDHwt rGBM via intratumoral and systemic immune activation. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT02303678 .

title: Real-world, digital-first delivery of GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy in women
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have demonstrated substantial weight reduction and cardiometabolic benefit in randomized trials; however, prospective implementation evidence from digital care models and female sex community populations remains limited. Here we report outcomes from an observational study of 8,127 women initiating GLP-1RA therapy (99.8% tirzepatide) through a structured digital program incorporating mandatory biochemical monitoring, weekly video-supported follow-up and clinician-guided dose titration in the UK. Mean weight reduction was 16.1 kg (95% confidence interval 15.9 to 16.2; P < 0.001), representing 15.5% of baseline weight; 83.1% achieved ≥10% and 22.4% achieved ≥20% weight loss, with consistent responses across age, baseline weight and socioeconomic strata. Among participants with paired biomarker data, mean glycated hemoglobin decreased by 3.3 mmol mol − 1 (95% confidence interval 3.1 to 3.4; P < 0.001), normalizing in 84.5% of those with baseline diabetes-range values and 96.3% with prediabetes, and lipid parameters improved significantly (reductions in total cholesterol of 0.77 mmol l − 1 , low-density lipoprotein cholesterol of 0.61 mmol l − 1 and triglycerides of 0.47 mmol l − 1 ). Retention was 91.4% at 6 months, with no serious treatment-related adverse events. These findings support the feasibility of delivering structured, digitally enabled obesity pharmacotherapy at scale and provide prospective real-world implementation evidence for this care model. Interpretation is limited by the observational design, absence of a comparator group, self-pay population and 6-month follow-up.

title: Conversational brain AI for adaptive epilepsy care
abstract: A small study shows that patients can help fine-tune their own seizure detectors by chatting with an AI agent. However, the more difficult challenge ahead is to build AI that responds appropriately.

title: A reality check for autoimmune CAR T cells
abstract: The hope with CAR T cell therapies for autoimmune disease is that they can reset the immune system and induce deep remission. But recent trial pauses have renewed concerns about safety, patient selection and acceptable risk.

title: Molecular predictors of minimal residual disease in newly diagnosed multiple myeloma treated with quadruplet therapy
abstract: Quadruplet therapy, combining anti-CD38 antibodies, immunomodulatory drugs, proteasome inhibitors and dexamethasone, is now the standard induction treatment for newly diagnosed multiple myeloma (NDMM). However, treatment response is heterogeneous and molecular predictors are needed to guide early therapeutic decisions. We performed integrated genomic, transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling of 423 tumor samples from patients with NDMM from the MIDAS cohort to characterize molecular heterogeneity and its association with measurable residual disease (MRD) after quadruplet induction with isatuximab, carfilzomib, lenalidomide and dexamethasone (Isa-KRd). Postinduction MRD-negativity rates varied significantly across gene expression subtypes, with HP1/HP3 and MS groups showing superior responses compared to the MF and CD2 subtypes. B cell differentiation was associated with MRD positivity, while proliferation and MYC programs were associated with MRD negativity. These MRD-associated transcriptomic features were independently validated in the CASSIOPEIA cohort. Whole-genome sequencing revealed both known (APOBEC mutagenesis, chromothripsis) and new genomic instability phenotypes validated in the MMRF cohort, including mismatch repair deficiency driven by pathogenic MSH2 mutations and a focal deletion signature linked to BRCA2 inactivation. New driver alterations were identified, including translocations activating IRAK1 and FOXR1 fusions, with independent validation. Genomic instability features and driver genes such as CCND1 and MYC correlated with differential MRD outcomes. DNA methylation profiling identified nine MRD-linked subgroups distinguished by the extent of hypomethylation in quiescent chromatin and cis / trans signatures of driver translocations. A multimodal random forest model integrating genomic, transcriptomic and epigenomic features predicted MRD status after induction, with an area under the curve of 0.77, outperforming clinical and genomic models, while providing comparable discrimination and improved calibration relative to the transcriptomic and epigenomic models. These findings define a multiomic classification of NDMM linked to Isa-KRd response. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04934475 .

title: Waiting to get sick enough
abstract: The liver can warn us of metabolic dysfunction long before serious consequences emerge. Why aren’t we listening?

title: Author Correction: FcRH5×CD3 bispecific antibody cevostamab in relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma: a phase 1 trial
abstract: In the version of the article initially published, in Extended Data Fig. 3b, the left x -axis label of both panels was “No 1q gain or amp” but should have been “1q normal”. This correction has been made to the HTML and PDF versions of the article.

title: Global and regional burden of measles and vaccine coverage among children under 5 years, 1990−2023: a Global Burden of Disease Study
abstract: Measles remains a leading cause of vaccine-preventable burden among children, particularly in low-income settings. Despite decades of progress, there are indications of measles resurgence due to stagnation in vaccine coverage. Here, using the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries and Risk Factors Study (GBD) 2023, we systematically assessed measles incidence, mortality, disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) and vaccine coverage (measles-containing vaccine 1 (MCV1) and measles-containing vaccine 2 (MCV2)) among children under 5 years of age across 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023. Between 1990 and 2019, global measles incidence and mortality declined by approximately 80% and 90%, respectively, but rebounded sharply after 2020, with 15.6 million cases and 118,000 deaths estimated in 2023 (+40% and +12% increases, respectively, between 2019 and 2023). Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia continue to bear the highest burden. Global MCV1 coverage rose from 67.2% in 1990 to 83.6% in 2019 but stalled and declined slightly to 81.0% by 2023; MCV2 coverage increased from 14.4% in 1990 to 68.4% in 2019 and reached 71.4% by 2023. Several regions remain well below the Immunization Agenda 2030 (IA2030) target of 90% coverage. The recent measles resurgence underscores the fragility of global immunization progress and the urgent need to restore routine vaccination, close immunity gaps and strengthen outbreak preparedness.

title: Global, regional and national burden of pertussis in 1990–2023: a Global Burden of Disease study
abstract: Despite long-standing immunization programs, pertussis remains a major cause of vaccine-preventable mortality, particularly among infants. Here we present a primary assessment of global pertussis incidence, mortality and disability-adjusted life years across 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023. We show that despite short-term pandemic-period fluctuations, the dominant global pattern from 1990 to 2023 was long-term decline: age-standardized mortality decreased by 61.2% and age-standardized incidence by 41.6%. Relative to the anomalously low pandemic-period estimates, incidence and mortality rebounded by 102.6% (95% uncertainty interval, 77.0–128.2%) and 66.1% (95% uncertainty interval, 2.4–174.5%), respectively, between 2020 and 2023. In 2023 alone, we estimated 18.9 million cases and 115,000 deaths attributable to pertussis. This burden remains profoundly inequitable and inversely correlated with the sociodemographic index; sub-Saharan Africa now accounts for roughly 65% of global deaths, with the highest population-adjusted risk concentrated among infants younger than 6 months. Our findings highlight a modeled geographic concentration of pertussis mortality and support strengthening timely infant vaccination, maternal immunization where recommended and feasible and robust surveillance in highly susceptible regions.

title: The need for resilience in global vaccination programs
abstract: New studies of trends in the global burden of measles and pertussis offer a reminder of how much vaccination has achieved and a warning of the need to build more resilient and sustainable vaccination programs.

title: Author Correction: Povorcitinib for hidradenitis suppurativa: the randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled STOP-HS1 and STOP-HS2 phase 3 trials
abstract: In the version of the article initially published, in the second paragraph of the “Patients” section of the Results, “Baseline disease characteristics were indicative of recalcitrant, longstanding HS (mean (range) disease duration, 9.7 (0.4−49.1)−10.8 (0.3−48.7) years)” should have read “Baseline disease characteristics were indicative of recalcitrant, longstanding HS (mean (range) disease duration, 9.7 (0.4−49.1)−10.8 (0.4−57.7) years)”. In the Fig. 1 legend, in footnote b , “In STOP-HS2, two patients discontinued after completing treatment through week 12: one discontinued due to physician decision, and one withdrew” should have read “In STOP-HS2, three patients discontinued after completing treatment through week 12: two discontinued due to physician decision, and one withdrew”; and footnote d was “Two patients discontinued after completing treatment through week 12; both withdrew” but should have been “One patient withdrew after completing treatment through week 12”. In Table 2, the superscript for the P values in STOP-HS1 for the 75 mg dose in the rows for ≥3-point decrease in Skin Pain NRS and Skin Pain NRS30 should be “ f ” rather than “ e ”. In Extended Data Fig. 5e, f, the grey dotted line between weeks 18 and 24 should have been blue and the values next to the week 6 dots should have been next to the week 12 dots. Additionally, in Supplementary Table 6A, the “Week 12” row of the “A75, Baseline A count, 3−5” section originally read “37.2 (16/43), 36.8 (25/68), 35.3 (18/51)” but should have read “36.8 (25/68), 35.3 (18/51), 37.2 (16/43)”. These corrections have been made to the HTML and PDF versions of the article.

Milk multi-omics links maternal health to infant growth
abstract: Researchers identify biomarkers that explain how maternal health is linked to mammary gland function, breast milk composition and infant growth, highlighting maternal nutrition as a public health priority.

title: Author Correction: β-catenin confers resistance to PI3K and AKT inhibitors and subverts FOXO3a to promote metastasis in colon cancer
Determinants of response to CAR T cell therapy in a multicenter, multi-trial cohort analysis of patients with lymphoma
abstract: In patients with non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) treated with chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy, factors associated with efficacy overlap with prognostic biomarkers. Currently, there is no consensus on optimal product characteristics. We analyzed the phenotypic attributes of the anti-CD19 CAR T therapy axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel) from 580 patients with NHL across multiple clinical trials with long-term follow-up (median, 41.9 months). A high proportion of naive-like (CCR7 + CD45RA + ) T cells was the most significant feature associated with prolonged progression-free survival (PFS; hazard ratio = 0.46, 95% confidence interval: 0.31−0.68, P = 9.8 × 10 −5 , high versus low naive-like T cell groups) without impacting safety. The relationship between naive-like T cells and efficacy was independent of tumor microenvironment characteristics (assessed in 112 patients). In multivariate models, the naive-like phenotype outperformed clinicopathologic features such as inflammatory markers and tumor burden, remaining significant after adjusting for product expansion. An inverse correlation was observed between prior lines of therapy and the proportion of naive-like T cells in both product and matched apheresis samples, suggesting a benefit of earlier intervention. The key findings were validated in an independent cohort of 203 patients treated with axi-cel-based therapy or brexucabtagene autoleucel. Mass cytometry by time-of-flight analysis of products from a subgroup of 116 patients confirmed an association between a CD8 naive-like T cell phenotype lacking expression of exhaustion markers, such as TIGIT, LAG-3 and PD-1, and PFS. The evidence generated by this study has the potential to advance the development of more effective cellular therapies.

title: The human microbiome and chronic disease: ten strategic priorities for research and public health
abstract: The human microbiome has emerged as one of the most consequential frontiers in biomedical science. An international group of leading microbiome scientists, convened by the US Department of Health and Human Services, presents a strategic vision for realizing its potential to transform public health.

title: Lymph node-targeted, mKRAS-specific amphiphile vaccine in pancreatic cancer: the randomized phase 2 AMPLIFY-7P trial
abstract: Camupepimut (ELI-002 7P) drives mutated KRAS (mKRAS)-specific T cell responses that correlated with disease-free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS) in patients with mKRAS pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC) in the phase 1 AMPLIFY-201 trial. In the phase 2 AMPLIFY-7P trial, patients with stage I-III KRAS-mutated PDAC without recurrence within 6 months of standard therapy were randomized 2:1 to camupepimut ( n = 96) or standard-of-care/observation ( n = 48). Stratification balanced nodal status. The primary DFS endpoint was not met (median 23.8 versus 21.2 months; HR 0.85, P = 0.5329). However, prespecified and exploratory analyses were informative. A numerical DFS advantage at 6 months of 14.0% (75.7% versus 61.7%; HR 0.55, P = 0.0557) corresponded to camupepimut dosing. Post hoc multivariate Cox regression analysis of DFS indicated an improved outcome for camupepimut (adjusted HR 0.47, P = 0.0086), a worse outcome for stage III disease (adjusted HR 2.29, P = 0.0127), an elevated baseline CA19-9 (adjusted HR 3.16, P < 0.0001) and baseline circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) positivity (adjusted HR 5.99, P < 0.0001). Prespecified subgroup analyses addressing prognostic and predictive factors suggested DFS benefit for camupepimut (ctDNA negative: HR 0.51, P = 0.0280; no prior radiation: HR 0.59, P = 0.0221). Exploratory analysis demonstrated that ex vivo mKRAS-specific T cell responses were robust (98.9%, 89/90) and associated with antigen spreading (86.7%, 13/15). In camupepimut-treated patients, mKRAS-specific T cell response >9.17-fold over baseline (82.2%, 74/90) correlated with improved DFS (HR 0.22, P < 0.0001), with the median DFS not reached versus 6.08 months for above and below 9.17-fold, respectively. Camupepimut safety was similar to observation, with grade ≥3 adverse events in 10.4% (10/96) versus 14.6% (7/48), and few serious AEs (6.3%, 6/96 versus 8.3%, 4/48; reflecting progression/surgical complication). These efficacy and immunogenicity signals will inform a refined strategy for a confirmatory phase 3 trial. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05726864 .

title: Bispecific dual T cell agonist invikafusp alfa in solid tumors: the phase 1/2 START-001 trial
abstract: Invikafusp alfa (invika), a first-in-class, bispecific, dual T cell agonistic antibody selectively targeting Vβ6/Vβ10 T cell subsets, is being evaluated in START-001, a multicenter phase 1/2 monotherapy trial in participants with mostly immune checkpoint blockade (ICB)-resistant, antigen-rich solid tumors. Primary outcomes were safety/tolerability and recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D) in phase 1 and anti-tumor activity in phase 2. As of 12 March 2025, phase 1 completed dose escalation ( n = 34) through dose levels of 0.01, 0.02, 0.04, 0.08, 0.12 and 0.16 mg kg −1 without reaching maximum tolerated dose, and initial phase 2 enrolled 18 participants. Two participants experienced reversible dose-limiting toxicities, one at each of the 0.08 mg kg −1 and 0.16 mg kg −1 dose levels. The most common treatment-related adverse event was cytokine release syndrome, mainly grades 1 and 2. No treatment-related deaths or non-laboratory grade 4 adverse events were reported. At the optimal biological doses (OBDs; 0.08 mg kg −1 and 0.12 mg kg −1 ) in combined phase 1 and phase 2 cohorts, the overall objective response rate was 14.8% (4/27), including confirmed partial responses in immunologically cold tumors, such as microsatellite stable colorectal cancer and programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1)-negative non-small cell lung cancer. No objective responses were seen at doses lower than 0.08 mg kg −1 . Invika selectively and potently expanded peripheral and intratumoral Vβ6/Vβ10 T cells, of a predominantly memory-like phenotype, dose-dependently, peaking at the OBDs. Pharmacodynamic increases in interferon-γ and soluble CD25 followed a similar pattern. Integrated analyses from safety, pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic and preliminary anti-tumor data supported the selection of 0.08 mg kg −1 as the RP2D. In conclusion, phase 1 of START-001 met its primary outcomes by demonstrating the acceptable safety profile of invika consistent with its mechanism of action and selecting an RP2D. Initial phase 2 results further corroborated the safety of invika and expanded its preliminary evidence of clinically meaningful anti-tumor activity in ICB-resistant solid tumors, supporting further evaluation in the ongoing phase 2. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05592626 .

title: Putting conversational AI to the test in primary care
abstract: A patient-facing conversational AI showed promising feasibility and safety in a single-center primary care setting, providing a basis for larger-scale evaluation.

title: Neoadjuvant nivolumab with or without visugromab in muscle-invasive bladder cancer: the phase 2a GDFATHER-NEO trial
abstract: Growth differentiation factor-15 (GDF-15) is overexpressed in muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) and was recently identified as a potential therapeutic target to overcome resistance to programmed cell death protein 1/programmed death ligand 1 (PDL1) blockade. We investigated the safety and efficacy of GDF-15 blockade in an exploratory, stratified, placebo-controlled, single-blinded, nonrandomized phase 2a trial (GDFATHER-NEO). Thirty-one cisplatin-ineligible or cisplatin-refusing patients with newly diagnosed MIBC (clinical T2–T4aN0M0) were stratified by tumor stage and PDL1 combined positive score (CPS) and allocated sequentially to receive three cycles of neoadjuvant nivolumab (N, 480 mg 4-weekly) plus the GDF-15-neutralizing antibody visugromab (V, 20 mg kg −1 4-weekly; n = 16) or placebo (P, n = 15), followed by radical cystectomy or repeat transurethral resection of the bladder tumor. Locally assessed pathologic complete response (pCR, ypT0N0/x) and Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors v1.1-based radiographic response served as dual primary endpoints. pCR was 33% (5 of 15, 95% confidence interval (CI) 12–62%) in patients receiving N + V versus 8% (1 of 13, 95% CI 0–36%) for N + P; major pathologic response was 60% (95% CI 32–84%) versus 23% (95% CI 5–54%), and radiographic overall response rate was 60% (95% CI 32–84%) versus 15% (95% CI 2–45%), respectively. Responses to N + V were associated with higher baseline densities of total and proliferating (Ki-67 + ) CD8 + T cells, but independent of CPS and baseline GDF-15 levels in serum and tumor. There were no treatment-related discontinuations or treatment-related delays to surgery; grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in two (13%) and three (20%) patients treated with N + V or N + P, respectively. These findings support further evaluation of visugromab in MIBC. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06059547 .

title: Relatlimab plus nivolumab versus nivolumab for advanced melanoma: 5-year survival and biomarker analyses of the phase 3 RELATIVITY-047 trial
abstract: Nivolumab plus relatlimab is approved for advanced melanoma based on the RELATIVITY-047 trial; however, long-term data are needed. Here we report data from RELATIVITY-047 with the longest follow-up at present. In this phase 2−3, double-blind trial, patients with metastatic/unresectable melanoma were randomized 1:1 to nivolumab 480 mg plus relatlimab 160 mg ( n = 355) or nivolumab 480 mg ( n = 359) intravenously every 4 weeks. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS) by blinded independent central review. Secondary endpoints were overall survival (OS), response and safety. Additional post hoc analyses, such as melanoma-specific survival (MSS) and exploratory biomarker analyses, are also reported. This analysis shows clear separation in survival curves with the largest absolute differences to date in PFS, OS and MSS. In this prespecified 5-year analysis, with a minimum follow-up of 57.3 months, nivolumab plus relatlimab demonstrated continued clinically significant benefit versus nivolumab for PFS (hazard ratio (HR) = 0.77; 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.65−0.92), OS (HR = 0.78; 95% CI: 0.64−0.95) and MSS (HR = 0.71; 95% CI: 0.57−0.88). The safety profile remained consistent with prior reports. Among biomarker-evaluable patients in the PD-L1 ≥1% subgroup, analyses revealed an association between worse outcomes with nivolumab and high peripheral or tumor LAG-3 + CD8 cell levels. The addition of relatlimab to nivolumab was associated with a lower prevalence of primary resistance than nivolumab alone. These data support the hypothesis that relatlimab can overcome LAG-3-mediated resistance to nivolumab and provide evidence for differential efficacy patterns observed across biomarker subgroups linked to primary versus acquired resistance states. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03470922 .

title: Neoadjuvant durvalumab plus chemotherapy in resectable or borderline resectable non-small-cell lung cancer: the phase 2 MDT-BRIDGE trial
abstract: The phase 2 MDT-BRIDGE study is investigating perioperative durvalumab plus neoadjuvant chemotherapy (AEGEAN regimen) in resectable and borderline resectable non-small-cell lung cancer and chemoradiotherapy (CRT) followed by consolidation durvalumab (PACIFIC regimen) in patients who become unresectable after neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy guided by multidisciplinary team assessments during the neoadjuvant period. The primary endpoint was the overall resection rate (descriptive with no formal hypothesis testing). Secondary endpoints included event-free survival, progression-free survival, pathological complete response rate (resectable patients cohort), circulating tumor DNA clearance between baseline and presurgery/pre-CRT and safety. Overall, 142 patients received neoadjuvant treatment; 64.8% and 35.2% were deemed resectable and borderline resectable at baseline, respectively. The overall resection rate (95% confidence interval) was 74.6% (66.7‒81.6) in a population that included more than one-third of patients with borderline resectable disease. R0 resection rate was 96.2% (90.6‒99.0) in those who underwent surgery. Overall, 131 (92.3%) patients had surgery ( n = 106) or CRT ( n = 25) after neoadjuvant treatment, and 117 (82.4%) patients received adjuvant ( n = 94) or consolidation ( n = 23) durvalumab. During adjuvant or consolidation durvalumab, maximum grade 3/4 adverse events occurred in 7.4% of resected patients and 17.4% of CRT-treated patients, with 8.5% and 13.0% discontinuing treatment due to adverse events. This multidisciplinary team-guided approach was feasible and enabled delivery of curative-intent treatment (surgery or CRT), followed by durvalumab in most patients, and demonstrated encouraging preliminary efficacy with a manageable adjuvant or consolidation safety profile that was consistent with prior studies. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05925530 .

title: Persistent and compartmentalized T cell immunity in ALS
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a fatal neurodegenerative disease increasingly linked to T cell responses, although the mechanisms driving T cell activation and disease progression remain unclear. Here we used single-cell RNA and T cell receptor sequencing, longitudinal immune profiling and imaging flow cytometry to identify long-lived intrathecal clonotypes and antigen-presenting cell–T cell complexes displaying features of immunological synapse formation, consistent with intrathecal antigen presentation. Higher frequencies of CD4 + effector, CD4 + regulatory and CD8 + T cells in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) were associated with slower disease progression, whereas increased circulating CD4 + effector and regulatory T cells were associated with faster progression. T cell clonotypes shared between blood and CSF exhibited distinct transcriptional states. Finally, frequencies of cytomegalovirus-specific T cells in CSF and anticytomegalovirus serum antibodies were correlated with faster progression and shorter survival in sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. These findings reveal compartmentalized immune dynamics, largely contrasting protective intrathecal responses with harmful systemic activation.

title: Metabolic heterogeneity of obesity
abstract: Multi-organ-system insulin resistance is the key pathogenic driver of obesity-related metabolic complications and diseases, such as atherogenic dyslipidemia, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and type 2 diabetes. However, there is considerable heterogeneity in insulin sensitivity among people with obesity. Some are considered to have metabolically healthy obesity, with normal insulin sensitivity in conjunction with normal fasting blood glucose, oral glucose tolerance, plasma lipid profile and intrahepatic triglyceride content. In this Review, we discuss metabolic differences at the cellular, organ-system and systemic levels between people with metabolically healthy and metabolically unhealthy obesity; we also discuss heterogeneity in the therapeutic effects of weight reduction. A better understanding of the differences between metabolically divergent groups and the physiological responses to weight loss can help identify the factors responsible for the link between excess adiposity and metabolic dysfunction and disease.

title: Author Correction: Toripalimab or placebo plus chemotherapy as first-line treatment in advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma: a multicenter randomized phase 3 trial
